newsitem.title: USA: Muni market feels disclosure growing pains - survey.
newsitem.headline: Muni market feels disclosure growing pains - survey.

text.p: Municipal market participants are experiencing substantial growing pains as they try to -- or in many cases resist -- adjusting to the SEC's two-year-old secondary market disclosure rule, a new industry survey released Thursday shows.

PSA The Bond Market Trade Association and the National Federation of Municipal Analysts found that 33 percent of respondents said it is harder now to get information that is not specifically required by the rule than it was before the Securities and Exchange Commission enacted it in 1994.

Twenty-five percent of respondents said the quality and quantity of information is worse, while 13 percent said it is better, said the groups, who debated the findings at a two-hour public symposium that they sponsored at PSA headquarters in New York City.

Sixty-eight percent of those responding to the survey said some issuers only will make annual financial statements and updated operating data available through national and state repositories, rather than directly, the two groups said.
And there are "substantial discrepancies" in the information that is available from all repositories, they said.
"This is a period of transition," said Catherine Spain, head of the Government Finance Officers Association's Washington office, during Thursday's panel discussion.
"It's fair to say that issuers are still grappling to understand the rule" and the federal securities laws on which it is based, she said. "It's been a major period of learning."

She said one of the problems is that many of the "trusted advisers" that issuers rely on, including bond lawyers and financial advisers, "have been equally in the dark" on the new rule. She added that there is a "lot of fear" about what the standards mean.

PSA President Heather Ruth said issuers' fears of "insider trading" is a continuous problem. Issuers have expressed concern that if they release data over the phone to individual investors, they could run afoul of federal insider trading restrictions, panelists said.
In other survey findings, PSA and the analysts said 15 percent of respondents said official statements are deteriorating and 12.4 percent said updated operating data is declining.
Twenty percent reported difficulty getting annual financial statements and 14.2 said they had trouble getting updated operating data, the groups said.

Sixty-nine percent of respondents said more issuers are incorporating financial documents by reference, which means higher costs for those trying to retrieve the information, the groups said. Twenty-eight percent said it also decreases overall quality or quantity of information, they added.

The study also found, "If there are disclosure problems by sector, they are coming from healthcare (22.5 percent say it is worse); housing (11 percent say it is worse); and student loans (10.7 percent say it is worse."
But health care and housing also appear to have the highest "better ratings," with 19 percent saying both sectors are better, the groups said.

The groups found that revenue bond issuers are providing annual financials and updated operating data quicker than issuers of tax-backed bonds, "thirty six percent in under six months versus 29 percent for tax backed (bonds)."
About 41 percent of each sector get the documents out in six to nine months, the survey found.

"Both groups of issuers have substanial numbers providing the information as late as nine months or more after the end of the fiscal year -- 22 percent of revenue bond issuers and 29 percent of tax backed bond issuers," the groups said.
The groups said 40 percent of respondents consider the timeframes "unacceptable."
The groups said industry is split on whether there is a difference in the quantity or quality of information on competitive and negotiated issues.
"For those who think there is a difference, 84 percent think negotiated disclosure is better," the groups said. "And 14 percent think the difference has increased since the rules went into effect."
